comment.value:
The work presents MedicalNarratives, a  dataset providing a large collection of spatially grounded medical images and text derived from medical videos, comprising over 4.7 million medical records, including 1M samples with spatial grounding via cursor traces.  The dataset is designed to offer a comprehensive view of patients' conditions through the integration of image and textual information. Through various vision-language research tasks, including semantic understanding and prediction, this work aims at supporting the development of radiology workflows aimed at automatic abnormality detection and diagnostic assistance.


The reviewers were generally positive towards the paper, acknowledging the contribuition of this work in providing a valuable resource for vision-language tasks, with some innovative features such as narration pointing behavioral traces. A few specific issues were raised in the review, especially concerning the unblanaced nature of the data and potential bias, the need for human annotations as a complement to model-based metrics, and that need to better clarify the contribution of the traces to support spatial grounding. 


The authors' response acknowledged the reviewers' comments and addressed them by providing more context about the dataset's real-world utility, highlighting its potential for improving radiology workflows such as abnormality detection and diagnostic assistance. Additionally, they emphasized the importance of human evaluation in complementing model-based metrics, acknowledging that it is a valuable aspect of assessing the performance of their tasks on the MedicalNarratives dataset. 


The reviewers appreciated the additional context and clarification of the rebuttal and confirmed their favorable attitude towards the paper. As a result, the reviewers maintained or even increased their initial score, demonstrating a general agreement on the quality and merit of the work. For this reason, the paper can be accepted to NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks Track.

===== FINAL UPDATE FROM DB Track PCs ====

The final decision for this paper has been taken by the program chairs after consultation with the SACs. All Senior Area Chairs have ranked papers according to the feedback from the AC during the review process. We decided to leave the original meta-review to reflect the opinion of the AC in light of the initial discussions with reviewers and SAC.

Since the AC felt that my comments were too brief, I have added a few more sentences. It is possible that the AC did not see my Final Justification. The authors have responded to the questions I raised regarding the dataset and code, which resolved my doubts. I have maintained a positive attitude toward this work from the beginning, and it is precisely because these fundamental doubts have been addressed that it deserves a score of 4.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------START

Sub-section:

Beyond retrieval/classification, the trace-aligned samples provide direct supervision for grounded language and localization tasks without dense masks. Following Localized Narratives [96, 122], each word/phrase co-occurring with a trace segment supplies weak phrase-region links for grounded captioning, referring expressions, and spatial relation inference. High-dwell (i.e. spatial regions where narrators focus on) segments of traces can be collapsed into pointing cues to train pointing-based medical MLMs, such as Molmo [31]. Because our traces are timestamped, the same supervision naturally extends to video: the trajectory of the cursor across frames yields spatiotemporal grounding suitable for dynamic "point-while-describe" models and temporal localization (e.g., axial CT sweeps or ultrasound). The dataset also supports tasks that predict spatial traces as additional loss objectives toward imbuing models with spatial understanding [129] and panoptic narrative grounding objectives [41] are directly enabled by these trace–text alignments.

For dense prediction and controllable generation, traces act as sparse supervision that can be transformed into inputs for interactive medical image segmentation (IMIS) models (e.g., as points/scribbles for ScribblePrompt) to bootstrap pseudo-masks and iteratively refine them [127]. Coupling trace spans with their co-mentioned phrases supplies approximately localized phrase labels for open-vocabulary detection/segmentation similar to phrase-region training [32, 38].

Finally, the same signals can guide where and what to synthesize in text-to-image/volume models, using trace/point conditioning alongside clinical text to localize clinical entities, while enabling spatially controllable medical report generation [68, 131, 113, 129].

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------END

We can't add figures in here, but we have figures of iterative refinement of traces to dense masks, as well as a figure outlining all spatial tasks this enables, which will be added in the appendix and referenced. We are also doing a final lit review to ensure we capture the full gamut of what MedNarratives could enable in case we have missed some.

Again, Thanks for your willingness to reconsider the evaluation based on these enhancements.

We thank reviewer bZ8z for their feedback and for highlighting the novelty of our narration-pointing approach, the strength of our data pipeline, and the potential for MedicalNarratives to support spatially grounded medical research.
We discuss the reviewers main concerns below:

**1. We explicitly acknowledge Limitation 1 and partially address it in the paper.**
 We agree this is an important concern. As noted in the Limitations section (Sec. 5, Point 1), our dataset does not include human-verified annotations for trace alignment. Nonetheless, we demonstrate trace utility via qualitative segmentation examples using the pretrained ScribblePrompt model in Figure 5. These results show that despite the absence of expert labels, our extracted traces can guide interactive segmentation models toward plausible object boundaries. We also provide further discussion and trace examples in the Appendix.

**2. Our methodology is grounded in effective spatial supervision paradigms.**
 Our pipeline builds on prior work in Localized Narratives [96, 122] and the think-aloud protocol used in clinical education. Instructors naturally verbalize diagnoses while pointing at relevant regions with their cursor—a behavior we leverage to create trace annotations that approximate spatial grounding. This connection is discussed in Sections 1 and 3.3 of the paper, and is central to our design.

**3. We address the implications of overrepresentation of pathological cases.** As acknowledged in Sec. 5, Point 2, our dataset overrepresents abnormal/pathological cases, which reflects real-world clinical imaging practices. We recognize that this may introduce bias, especially in clinical support settings. That said, GENMEDCLIP shows strong generalization across diverse medical domains, including tasks where healthy or borderline samples are prevalent (e.g., Isic, VinDr-CXR), suggesting robustness even in the presence of this bias.

**4. Trace-based supervision is already used for segmentation prompts.**
 Figure 5 shows how we convert raw trace points into segmentation prompts using ScribblePrompt, yielding interpretable masks. While not intended as a benchmark, these examples illustrate the feasibility of using trace signals for dense tasks like segmentation. As discussed in Sec. 5, we see this as a proof of concept and a promising foundation for future spatially-aware models.

We do not claim that the current traces fully support precision segmentation or detection tasks. Rather, we position them as a scalable, weak spatial supervision signal—valuable in a domain where expert labeling is costly and sparse.

rebuttal.value:
We thank reviewer MGsd for recognizing the scale and uniqueness of our MedicalNarratives dataset and its potential impact on the medical vision-language research.

The main concern raised is the lack of validation for the claim that traces can improve spatial reasoning. We provide clarifications addressing this concern below:

**1. We use traces as segmentation prompts as a proof of concept.** While our primary evaluations focus on retrieval and classification, we also demonstrate the potential spatial utility of traces through using ScribblePrompt in Figure 5. These results show that the trace data can guide segmentation tasks. We agree validating the value of these traces is of crucial concern and explicitly note it in the Limitations section (Sec. 5, Point 3). 

**2. Our methodology is aligned with prior work with trace-style supervision.** Our pipeline is inspired by Localized Narratives [96, 122], a dataset that has demonstrated utility for training spatially-aware models without explicit segmentation masks. In Section 1, we highlight how our design leverages the think-aloud behavior of experts (e.g., pointing while narrating), which has proven effective in spatial grounding across other domains.

**3. Our dataset is designed to unlock spatial reasoning in future work.**
Though we do not benchmark tasks like segmentation or detection, we hope the dataset enables others to explore grounded captioning, visual grounding, or spatially controllable report generation, tasks that are explicitly mentioned in our Discussion (Sec. 5). Additionally, Figure 1 and the Appendix provide examples of traces aligned with localized medical image regions, further suggesting the utility of these signals.

We emphasize that we do not claim the traces are already optimized for spatial modeling. Instead, we argue that they provide scalable spatial supervision, which is valuable given the high cost of expert annotation. 

We hope this clarifies our position and appreciate the reviewer’s call to further strengthen the spatial validation in future iterations of this work.

summary.value: This submission presents MEDICALNARRATIVES, a large-scale multimodal dataset designed to support medical vision-language research. The dataset consists of 4.7 million image-text pairs, of which 1 million samples are enriched with spatial grounding in the form of cursor traces. These are extracted from medical instructional videos and scientific articles, representing 12 different medical imaging modalities. The authors introduce a data curation pipeline that processes unstructured video and article sources by applying speech recognition, language correction, keyframe selection, and cursor trace localization. To assess the value of this dataset, the authors pretrain a contrastive vision-language model called GENMEDCLIP, and evaluate it across 29 downstream medical datasets. Results show improvements in zero-shot classification, cross-modal retrieval, and supervised learning settings over prior models.

strengths_contributions.value: The paper introduces MEDICALNARRATIVES, a large-scale, multimodal dataset containing 4.7M image-text pairs, including 1M samples with spatial grounding via cursor traces. This is a notable contribution to the medical vision-language research community, offering both scale and richness in spatial-textual alignment, which is relatively rare in existing datasets.

limitations_weaknesses.value: The most important problem is that while the authors argue that the trace data supports spatial grounding, this claim is not empirically validated. All experiments focus on classification and retrieval, and no spatially-grounded task (e.g., segmentation, pointing, report generation with spatial cues) is included to substantiate the benefit of trace supervision. As such, the core value proposition—that traces enhance spatial reasoning—remains speculative and unproven in the current study.

summary.value: This submission introduces a dataset of medical narratives, which consist of millions of medical image-text pairs annotated by localized pointer traces in image space. The pointer traces enable spatial grounding of medical concepts, which the authors demonstrate is able to translate to better vision-language embedding models.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. I appreciate the Limitations section in the manuscript, especially point (2) in line 300. This limitation is important but I understand there is very little the authors can do to overcome this, and appreciate the discussion to this effect.
2. The benefits of using the dataset proposed by the authors is well-demonstrated experimentally in Table 2 and 3. The authors do remark that they are not able to run multiple seeds for statistical significance in point 7 of the checklist - however, I don't think this is a large concern given that CLIP experiments typically have small error bars and the strength of the experimental results that are reported.
3. The supplementary material is extensive and detailed, which I think will be very helpful reference material for future researchers that would like to take advantage of the dataset.
4. The dataset includes many of the components of medical narratives that I believe are often missing in existing datasets: it supports multimodal inference which simulates the ability of clinicians to look through multiple imaging studies to arrive at a clinical narrative, and also includes video + scrolling through the scans, which again is representative of clinical reasoning.

limitations_weaknesses.value: Incidentally, each major question/comment I had on the submission was addressed sufficiently later in the manuscript upon further reading, to the point where there were no major weaknesses I could identify with this work after reading it from beginning to end. I include some clarifying questions/minor limitations in the "Additional Feedback" section, although I don't think any of these are significant enough to preclude acceptance. In general, I think this is a technically solid and significant contribution that would be of interest to researchers. My only caveat is that I am less versed in the medical multi-modal literature, and so defer points related to this to the expertise of the other reviewers.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

ethical_comments.value: The authors make use of existing publicly available data, so I don't think this work introduces any new ethical concerns.

dataset_code_comments.value: I am able to view the dataset without issues on HuggingFace - however, given the size of the dataset I am not able to download it locally. The presentation and formatting of the dataset on HuggingFace seems to be standard though.

additional_feedback.value:
5. It might be helpful to have a smaller, representative subset of the data in the same format as the complete dataset for researchers to experiment with it locally.
6. For future work on leveraging the dataset for training/evaluating VLMs, it may be worth including some discussion on whether metadata like publication date of the individual data is available to help control for data leakage.

final_justification.value:
I was previously in support of accepting this work prior to the rebuttal period, and still remain in support of accepting this work after considering the additional discussion from the authors and other reviewers.

That being said, I believe my initial review did not consider some of the points raised by some of the other reviewers that, in hindsight, are well-taken and important considerations. I specifically wanted to comment on the following:

  1. **Overrepresentation of Pathological Cases (Reviewer bZ8z)**: I definitely agree with Reviewer bZ8z on this, and hope the authors discuss this in additional detail in their manuscript as an important limitation. This is a common problem in medical datasets - if a dataset is planned to be made publicly available with minimal access restrictions (as in this case), then they must be derived from publicly available sources like PubMed which are obviously biased towards pathological cases that are "noteworthy enough" of publication. Any "real-world" dataset from, say, an academic hospital would almost certainly be impossible to be made publicly available from my experience. I do not necessarily agree with the authors' rationale that this "reflects real-world imaging practices" - rather, it seems more like an inevitability with most clinical datasets, and also can be justified because it is more important to get hard cases wrong than easy cases (since I believe easy cases would not benefit much from VLM insight).
  2. **Lack of Human-Annotated Bounding Boxes**: This was a consistently voiced concern shared by both Reviewer bZ8z and MGsd, and more broadly the concern of human expert verification was shared by all three other reviewers. Scalable tracing of human pointer annotation is challenging and I still think the approach made by the authors is reasonable for the task at hand. That being said, I agree with the other Reviewers that requesting the help of a few medical experts to review even a small random sample of the traces for accuracy and clinical validity would have further strengthened this work.

In summary, while I do believe that there are some additional drawbacks with this work as outlined by the other Reviewers, I personally still believe that they are not significant enough to preclude acceptance. As a result, I am still in favor of accepting this work.

summary.value:
This paper aims to address the bottleneck in medical vision-language tasks caused by the lack of spatial annotations and high-quality cross-modal image-text pairs. It introduces MEDICALNARRATIVES, a large-scale medical multimodal dataset comprising 4.7 million image-text pairs spanning 12 medical subdomains. The images are sourced from two main channels: YouTube medical instructional videos (unstructured, with narration and cursor behaviors) and PubMed scientific literature (structured image-caption pairs).

To process video data, the authors employ automatic speech recognition (Whisper), LLM-based text correction, YOLO-based image denoising, and cursor trace extraction using SSIM combined with face masking. Drawing inspiration from the "Think-aloud Protocol" and "Localized Narratives", the dataset captures natural semantic grounding between visual regions and textual descriptions through synchronized narration and cursor movements.

In addition, the authors train three variants of a CLIP-based model (with ViT and GPT2/BioMedBERT backbones), and evaluate them on a benchmark covering 11 medical domains. The proposed model, GENMEDCLIP, significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art models such as BIOMEDCLIP on both zero-shot classification and cross-modal retrieval, achieving over 26% improvement on average in the zero-shot retrieval task.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. This dataset innovatively incorporates "narration-pointing" behavioral traces from medical instructional videos. By automatically detecting cursor movements and spoken descriptions during lectures, it establishes a natural spatial alignment between image regions and semantic content. Compared to traditional medical image-text pairs that lack localization information, this mechanism offers a low-cost, highly scalable source of spatial supervision, effectively supporting tasks such as localization, segmentation, and captioning in medical imaging.
2. The data is sourced from both YouTube videos and PubMed articles, encompassing both structured and unstructured information. The authors design a comprehensive and scalable data curation pipeline, which includes speech transcription, terminology correction, image denoising, trace extraction, and modality alignment. This ensures feasible quality control at scale and establishes a strong paradigm for the standardization of future multimodal medical datasets.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. The paper explicitly states that the dataset does not include human-annotated bounding boxes or segmentation masks. This makes it difficult to assess the alignment accuracy between the extracted traces and the actual target regions, thereby limiting the dataset’s usability and reliability for high-precision dense prediction tasks such as semantic segmentation and object detection.
2. Since medical imaging is typically performed based on clinical suspicion, the dataset inevitably overrepresents pathological or abnormal cases during its construction. This distributional shift may introduce biases during model training, potentially undermining the model's generalization and robustness on healthy or borderline cases—posing a significant risk for clinical decision support systems.

summary.value: This paper introduces a new multimodal medical benchmark dataset, MedicalNarratives, which includes 46,727 pairs of radiology images and corresponding reports. Notably, the reports are structurally complete and divided into five main sections: Indication, Comparison, Findings, Impression, and Others. The authors propose a dual-level contrastive learning framework that jointly trains on both (image, full report) and (image, report section) pairs, aiming to more effectively capture the alignment between images and textual information.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. Compared with traditional datasets that only provide the impression section, MedicalNarratives includes structurally complete radiology reports, divided into five common clinical sections. This enhances control over linguistic granularity and supports better adaptability for multi-task learning.
2. Diverse downstream task evaluations are provided.
3. The data sources are clearly described, properly de-identified, and ethically approved.
4. The dataset and research design are both interesting—through visual exploration, corresponding textual descriptions can be generated, which is highly beneficial for clinical education and has meaningful real-world utility.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. After splitting the reports into different paragraph categories, is there any issue of insufficient or imbalanced data structure? It is recommended to supplement and explain this point.

2. Although many tasks are designed, it is still necessary to clarify the direct connection between these tasks and real-world radiology workflows (such as abnormality detection or diagnostic assistance). It is suggested to include relevant clinical motivations and explanations in the introduction and discussion sections.

3. Some tasks do not include consistency evaluation with clinical experts. It is recommended to introduce human evaluation to supplement the model-based metrics.

title.value: MedicalNarratives: Connecting Medical Vision and Language with Localized Narratives

abstract.value: Multi-modal models are data hungry. While datasets with natural images are abundant, medical image datasets can not afford the same luxury. To enable representation learning for medical images at scale, we turn to YouTube, a platform with a large reservoir of open-source medical pedagogical videos. We curate MedicalNarratives, a dataset 4.7M medical image-text pairs, with 1M samples containing dense annotations in the form of traces spatial traces (and bounding boxes), and 118K videos centered on the trace event (with aligned text), enabling spatiotemporal grounding beyond single frames. Similar to think-aloud studies where instructors speak while hovering their mouse cursor movements over relevant image regions, 1M images in MedicalNarratives contains localized mouse traces in image pixels, creating a spatial association between the text and pixels. To evaluate the utility of MedicalNarratives, we train GenMedClip with a CLIP-like objective using our dataset spanning 12 medical domains. GenMedClip outperforms previous state-of-the-art models on all 12 domains on a newly constructed medical imaging benchmark. Data, demo, code, and models will be made available.

Only if no qualified reviewer exists in the author list, nominate the best-qualified author for consideration by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. In addition, note that any author listed on 4 or more papers will be automatically regarded as a reviewer unless they are already serving as a reviewer, AC, SAC, or other roles in the Organization Committee. Failure to assign a qualified reviewer when one is available in the author list may result in desk rejection. Please enter an email address or an OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors (separate by comma if more than one nominations).

responsible_reviewing.description: We acknowledge that every author on the program committee is obligated to conduct responsible reviewing according to the policy designed by the PC Chairs and relevant members of the organizing committee. **Failure to do so may result in desk rejection or other serious consequences.**
